questions.prompt: What does an embedding model output for a piece of text?
questions.explanation: An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector; texts with related meaning point in similar directions. Individual dimensions are not human-readable features.

questions.prompt: Claude itself is the model you call to produce embeddings for vector search.
questions.explanation: False. Claude is a generative model. For embeddings you use a dedicated embedding model, for example Voyage AI (which Anthropic's docs point to), other hosted endpoints or local sentence-transformers models.

questions.prompt: Which kind of query are pure vector searches typically weakest at?
options: Exact identifiers such as error codes, SKUs and names
questions.explanation: Embeddings capture meaning, not exact strings, so error codes and IDs are a weak spot. Hybrid search adds keyword (BM25) matching for them.

questions.prompt: After normalising every vector to length 1, which statement is true?
questions.explanation: For unit vectors a·b / (|a||b|) = a·b. Euclidean distance still works and ranks results the same as cosine for unit vectors.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS search returns a chunk from another customer's documents. Which control was missing?
options: Metadata filtering by tenant/permissions at query time
questions.explanation: Similarity search does not know about access rights. Filtering on tenant and permission metadata must be part of every query; ignoring it is a listed mistake.

questions.prompt: For three queries the relevant document appeared at ranks 1, 3 and not in the results. What is the MRR?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal ranks are 1, 1/3 and 0 (not found). Mean = (1 + 0.333 + 0) / 3 ≈ 0.444.

questions.prompt: Whole 80-page manuals were embedded as single vectors. Search returns the right manual sometimes, but the answer section is rarely found. Why?
options: The documents exceed the model's input limit (silently truncated) and one vector blurs many topics; chunk the documents instead
Cosine should be replaced by dot product
questions.explanation: Embedding huge documents loses everything past the input limit and averages meaning across topics. Chunking into passages gives precise, retrievable units.

questions.prompt: You switch from brute-force search to an HNSW index; latency drops 20x but a few labelled queries now miss their document. What is the right interpretation?
options: ANN trades a little recall for speed; measure recall@k on the labelled set and tune index parameters until it meets your target
questions.explanation: Approximate indexes search a fraction of vectors, so slightly lower recall is expected and tunable. A labelled evaluation set tells you whether the trade-off is acceptable.

questions.prompt: After upgrading the embedding model, what must happen? Select all that apply.
options: Re-embed all documents with the new model
Embed queries with the same new model
Keep old document vectors to save cost
questions.explanation: Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so documents and queries must share one model. Re-run evaluation to confirm quality. Mixing old and new vectors is the classic failure.

coding.title: recall@k and MRR
coding.prompt:
Write `retrieval_metrics(results, relevant, k)` where `results` maps a query id to its ranked list of doc ids and `relevant` maps a query id to the set of relevant doc ids. Return `(recall_at_k, mrr)` rounded to 4 decimals:

- recall@k: fraction of queries with at least one relevant doc in the top k.
- MRR: mean over queries of 1/rank of the first relevant doc (rank starts at 1; 0 if none appears anywhere in the list).
coding.explanation: recall@k asks 'did we find it within budget?', while MRR rewards ranking it near the top, which matters because the LLM sees the top chunks first. Tracking both on a labelled set tells you whether a change (new embedding model, chunking, reranker) helped.
hints: Loop over queries; check `ranked[:k]` for recall.
Use `enumerate(ranked, 1)` and break at the first relevant doc for MRR.
Divide both totals by the number of queries.
